title: “Save, Lord: let the king hear us when we call” — the Greek asks the Lord to save the king
summary: The KJV ends the psalm with a call to the Lord to save, and then asks that the king hear us. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, asks the Lord to save the king and to hear us; the king is the one saved, not the one who hears.
text: KJV Psalms 20:9: “Save, Lord: let the king hear us when we call.” Hebrew (WLC) 20:10: יְהוָ֥ה הֹושִׁ֑יעָה הַ֝מֶּ֗לֶךְ יַעֲנֵ֥נוּ בְיֹום־קָרְאֵֽנוּ׃. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 19:10: Κύριε σῶσον τὸν βασιλέα καὶ ἐπάκουσον ἡμῶν, ἐν ᾗ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπικαλεσώμεθά σε. [Lord, save the king, and hear us on whatever day we call upon you]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/20/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA019.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV the king is the subject of the second clause: “let the king hear us when we call”. In the Greek the king is the object of the first clause, σῶσον τὸν βασιλέα, “save the king”, and the one who hears is the same Lord who is addressed: ἐπάκουσον ἡμῶν, “hear us”. The two verses therefore name different people as the one who hears the prayer, and they give the king a different place in the line, as the one acted upon in the Greek and as the one who hears in the KJV.
scope: T applies at Psalm 20:9 (Greek 19:10) and only to the place of “the king” in the line. The Hebrew words are the same words in the same order for a reader of either version, and the record does not say which way the Hebrew must be divided or read; that is a question for a Hebrew reader and is not decided here. Both texts address the Lord at the start. The verse is a prayer in verse. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: “I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever” — the Hebrew and the Greek say “for length of days”
summary: At Psalm 23:6 the KJV has the speaker dwelling in the house of the Lord “for ever”. The Hebrew phrase is לְאֹרֶךְ יָמִים, and the Septuagint has εἰς μακρότητα ἡμερῶν; both are “to length of days”. The KJV uses “for ever” at 93:5 for the same two Hebrew words.
text: KJV Psalm 23:6: “Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever.” Hebrew (WLC) 23:6: אַ֤ךְ ׀ טֹ֤וב וָחֶ֣סֶד יִ֭רְדְּפוּנִי כָּל־יְמֵ֣י חַיָּ֑י וְשַׁבְתִּ֥י בְּבֵית־יְ֝הוָ֗ה לְאֹ֣רֶךְ יָמִֽים׃. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 22:6: Καὶ τὸ ἔλεός σου καταδιώξεταί με πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς μου, καὶ τὸ κατοικεῖν με ἐν οἴκῳ Κυρίου εἰς μακρότητα ἡμερῶν. [and my dwelling in the house of the Lord is to length of days]. KJV Psalm 93:5: “Thy testimonies are very sure: holiness becometh thine house, O Lord, for ever.” Hebrew (WLC) 93:5: עֵֽדֹתֶ֨יךָ ׀ נֶאֶמְנ֬וּ מְאֹ֗ד לְבֵיתְךָ֥ נַאֲוָה־קֹ֑דֶשׁ יְ֝הוָ֗ה לְאֹ֣רֶךְ יָמִֽים׃. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 92:5: Τὰ μαρτύριά σου ἐπιστώθησαν σφόδρα· τῷ οἴκῳ σου πρέπει ἁγίασμα, Κύριε, εἰς μακρότητα ἡμερῶν. […holiness becomes your house, Lord, to length of days]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/23/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/93/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA022.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA092.htm.
reasoning: The KJV’s “for ever” names unending time. The two Hebrew words at the end of each verse are a noun meaning length or longness and a noun meaning days, and the Greek renders them with the same two ideas, μακρότητα and ἡμερῶν. The KJV prints “length of days” at other places where the same Hebrew pair stands, for example Psalm 21:4 beside “for ever and ever” in the same verse, where the Hebrew has a different word for “for ever and ever”. A reader of the KJV at 23:6 and 93:5 therefore reads a promise without end; a reader of the Hebrew or the Greek reads a promise that lasts a long span of days.
scope: T applies at Psalm 23:6 and 93:5 and only to the closing phrase. “Length of days” is an idiom that a lexicon may allow to mean a lifetime or a long life, and the KJV’s “for ever” may be its reading of that idiom; the record does not say that “for ever” is wrong, only that the KJV prints a different expression from the one the Hebrew and the Greek print. It does not rule on what the psalmist meant, or on whether other passages promise dwelling without end. The claim about Psalm 21:4 is asserted from the packaged KJV and the Hebrew text of that verse and was not separately opened as a lexicon entry. title: “He gathereth the waters of the sea together as an heap” — the Greek has a wineskin
summary: The KJV says God gathers the waters of the sea together as a heap. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, has ὡσεὶ ἀσκόν, which Brenton prints as “as in a bottle”: the waters are gathered as into a skin container.
text: KJV Psalms 33:7: “He gathereth the waters of the sea together as an heap: he layeth up the depth in storehouses.” Hebrew (WLC) 33:7: כֹּנֵ֣ס כַּ֭נֵּד מֵ֣י הַיָּ֑ם נֹתֵ֖ן בְּאֹצָרֹ֣ות תְּהֹומֹֽות׃. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 32:7: Συνάγων ὡσεὶ ἀσκὸν ὕδατα θαλάσσης, τιθεὶς ἐν θησαυροῖς ἀβύσσους. [Gathering the waters of the sea as a wineskin, putting the deeps in storehouses]. The Greek ἀσκός is the word for a leather bag or wineskin, and Brenton’s English prints “bottle”. The two texts give two pictures of how the sea is gathered, as a mound in the KJV and as the contents of a container in the Greek.

title: “The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger” — the Greek has the rich becoming poor
summary: At Psalm 34:10 the KJV has the young lions lacking and suffering hunger, while those who seek the Lord lack no good thing. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, has πλούσιοι, “the rich”, who have become poor and have been hungry.
text: KJV Psalms 34:10: “The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the Lord shall not want any good thing.” Hebrew (WLC) 34:11: כְּ֭פִירִים רָשׁ֣וּ וְרָעֵ֑בוּ וְדֹרְשֵׁ֥י יְ֝הוָ֗ה לֹא־יַחְסְר֥וּ כָל־טֹֽוב׃. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/34/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA033.htm.
reasoning: The KJV sets one group, the young lions, against those who seek the Lord. The Greek sets another group, the rich, against the same seekers. A lion is an animal and a rich man is a person, so the group said to go hungry is not the same in the two texts. The Greek also says the hungry ones “have become poor”, ἐπτώχευσαν, where the KJV says they “lack”.

title: “The transgression of the wicked saith within my heart” — the Greek says “within himself”
summary: The KJV has the transgression of the wicked speaking “within my heart”, so the speaker’s heart is the place. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, has the lawless man saying “in himself”, ἐν ἑαυτῷ, so the wicked man’s own thought is the place.
text: KJV Psalms 36:1: “The transgression of the wicked saith within my heart, that there is no fear of God before his eyes.” Hebrew (WLC) 36:2: נְאֻֽם־פֶּ֣שַׁע לָ֭רָשָׁע בְּקֶ֣רֶב לִבִּ֑י אֵֽין־פַּ֥חַד אֱ֝לֹהִ֗ים לְנֶ֣גֶד עֵינָֽיו׃. reasoning: In the KJV the heart in which the oracle is heard is the psalmist’s: “within my heart”. In the Greek the speech is inside the wicked man: φησὶν ὁ παράνομος … ἐν ἑαυτῷ, “the lawless man says … in himself”. The two verses locate the speech in different persons. The Greek also turns the opening “transgression of the wicked saith” into a sentence with the lawless man as the subject of the verb.

title: “Thou makest his beauty to consume away like a moth” — the Greek has a spider’s web

text: KJV Psalms 39:11: “When thou with rebukes dost correct man for iniquity, thou makest his beauty to consume away like a moth: surely every man is vanity. Selah.” Hebrew (WLC) 39:12: בְּֽתֹוכָ֘חֹ֤ות עַל־עָוֹ֨ן ׀ יִסַּ֬רְתָּ אִ֗ישׁ וַתֶּ֣מֶס כָּעָ֣שׁ חֲמוּדֹ֑ו אַ֤ךְ הֶ֖בֶל כָּל־אָדָ֣ם סֶֽלָה׃. [With rebukes for iniquity you have chastened a man, and you have melted his soul away like a spider’s web; only in vain is every man troubled]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/39/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA038.htm.

title: “Neither have our steps declined from thy way” — the Greek has God turning aside their paths
summary: The KJV has the people saying their steps have not declined from God’s way. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, has them saying that God has turned their paths aside from his way.
text: KJV Psalms 44:18: “Our heart is not turned back, neither have our steps declined from thy way;” Hebrew (WLC) 44:19: לֹא־נָסֹ֣וג אָחֹ֣ור לִבֵּ֑נוּ וַתֵּ֥ט אֲשֻׁרֵ֗ינוּ מִנִּ֥י אָרְחֶֽךָ׃. [And our heart did not turn back; and you turned our paths aside from your way]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/44/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA043.htm.
reasoning: The two texts agree that their heart did not turn back. They then differ on the second half. In the KJV the people did not turn aside: “neither have our steps declined”. In the Greek the verb is ἐξέκλινας, “you turned aside”, in the second person, with “our paths” as its object: God is the one who turned their paths from his way. A sentence that denies any turning on the people’s part in the KJV becomes in the Greek a sentence that says the Lord himself turned them.
scope: T applies at Psalm 44:18 (Greek 43:19) and to who turns the steps and whether the clause is a denial. title: “Slay them not, lest my people forget” — the Greek has “lest they forget thy law”
summary: At Psalm 59:11 the KJV prays that the enemies not be slain, lest “my people” forget. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, prays that they not be killed, lest they, the enemies, forget “thy law”, τοῦ νόμου σου.
text: KJV Psalms 59:11: “Slay them not, lest my people forget: scatter them by thy power; and bring them down, O Lord our shield.” Hebrew (WLC) 59:12: אַל־תַּהַרְגֵ֤ם ׀ פֶּֽן־יִשְׁכְּח֬וּ עַמִּ֗י הֲנִיעֵ֣מֹו בְ֭חֵילְךָ וְהֹורִידֵ֑מֹו מָֽגִנֵּ֣נוּ אֲדֹנָֽי׃. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 58:12: Μὴ ἀποκτείνῃς αὐτοὺς, μήποτε ἐπιλάθωνται τοῦ νόμου σου· διασκόρπισον αὐτοὺς ἐν τῇ δυνάμει σου, καὶ κατάγαγε αὐτοὺς ὁ ὑπερασπιστής μου Κύριε. [Do not kill them, lest they forget your law; scatter them by your power, and bring them down, Lord my defender]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/59/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA058.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV the ones who might forget are the psalmist’s own people, and what they might forget is left unsaid. In the Greek the ones who might forget are the enemies themselves, αὐτοὺς … ἐπιλάθωνται, and what they would forget is the Lord’s law. The two verses therefore name different forgetters and a different thing forgotten. Brenton’s own note says some manuscripts of the Greek read λαοῦ, “people”.
scope: T applies at Psalm 59:11 (Greek 58:12) and to who forgets and what is forgotten. Both texts continue with “scatter them by thy power”. The Hebrew quoted has עַמִּי, “my people”. The note about a variant reading in the Greek is Brenton’s own and was read in the fetched English page; it means that not every witness to the Greek has “law”. The record does not say which reading is original. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. Psalm numbers in that edition follow the Greek numbering, so the chapter and verse numbers of the Greek differ from the KJV’s, and the Greek verse is cited by its own number. title: The earth shook — “the foundations also of the hills moved” (Psalm 18:7), “the foundations of heaven moved” (2 Samuel 22:8)
summary: Psalm 18 and 2 Samuel 22 give the same song of David. In the shaking of the earth Psalm 18:7 has the foundations of the hills moved, and 2 Samuel 22:8 has the foundations of heaven moved.
text: KJV Psalm 18:7: “Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations also of the hills moved and were shaken, because he was wroth.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 18:8: וַתִּגְעַ֬שׁ וַתִּרְעַ֨שׁ ׀ הָאָ֗רֶץ וּמֹוסְדֵ֣י הָרִ֣ים יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַ֝יִּתְגָּֽעֲשׁ֗וּ כִּי־חָ֥רָה לֹֽו׃. KJV 2 Samuel 22:8: “Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of heaven moved and shook, because he was wroth.” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 22:8: [וַתְגָּעַשׁ כ] (וַיִּתְגָּעַ֤שׁ ק) וַתִּרְעַשׁ֙ הָאָ֔רֶץ מֹוסְדֹ֥ות הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַיִּֽתְגָּעֲשׁ֖וּ כִּֽי־חָ֥רָה לֹֽו׃. reasoning: The two verses are the same line of the same song, introduced in 2 Samuel 22:1 as the words David spoke on the day the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. In Psalm 18 the things that shake are the foundations of the hills (הָרִים). In 2 Samuel 22 they are the foundations of heaven (הַשָּׁמַיִם). Hills belong to the earth and heaven does not, so the two printings do not name the same foundations.

title: At the Lord’s rebuke “the channels of waters were seen” (Psalm 18:15); “the channels of the sea appeared” (2 Samuel 22:16)

title: “There were they in great fear: for God is in the generation of the righteous” (Psalm 14:5) and “…where no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee” (Psalm 53:5)
summary: Psalm 14 and Psalm 53 are nearly the same psalm. Where Psalm 14:5–6 says that God is in the generation of the righteous and that the wicked shamed the poor man’s counsel, Psalm 53:5 says that God scattered the bones of the one who encamped against his people and put them to shame.
text: KJV Psalm 14:5: “There were they in great fear: for God is in the generation of the righteous.” 14:6: “Ye have shamed the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 14:5–6: שָׁ֤ם ׀ פָּ֣חֲדוּ פָ֑חַד כִּֽי־אֱ֝לֹהִ֗ים בְּדֹ֣ור צַדִּֽיק׃ / עֲצַת־עָנִ֥י תָבִ֑ישׁוּ כִּ֖י יְהוָ֣ה מַחְסֵֽהוּ׃. KJV Psalm 53:5: “There were they in great fear, where no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee: thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 53:6: שָׁ֤ם ׀ פָּֽחֲדוּ־פַחַד֮ לֹא־הָ֪יָה֫ פָ֥חַד כִּֽי־אֱלֹהִ֗ים פִּ֭זַּר עַצְמֹ֣ות חֹנָ֑ךְ הֱ֝בִשֹׁ֗תָה כִּֽי־אֱלֹהִ֥ים מְאָסָֽם׃. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/PSA014.htm and https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/PSA053.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/14/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/53/.
reasoning: After the same opening, the two psalms diverge. Psalm 14 gives two short lines: the wicked feared, because God is with the righteous generation; the wicked shamed the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge. Psalm 53 gives one longer line in which there was fear where no fear was, God scattered the bones of the one encamped against the people, and the one addressed has put them to shame because God has despised them. The Lord (Hebrew יְהוָה) is the refuge in 14:6, while the divine name used throughout Psalm 53 is God (אֱלֹהִים). The two psalms differ in who shamed whom: the wicked shamed the poor man’s counsel in 14:6, and the encamped enemy were put to shame in 53:5.
scope: This sets two psalms beside each other as the KJV gives them. It does not say either is in error. The psalms may be two forms of one song, and the books do not say which came first. The difference in the divine name, Lord against God, is a known feature of this group of psalms and is not claimed as a contradiction. Only the KJV and the Hebrew wording of these verses were compared; the Greek of Psalms 14 and 53 was not read in full, and Psalm 14:3 has its own published record. title: “Glory and honour are in his presence; strength and gladness are in his place” (1 Chronicles 16:27) and “Honour and majesty are before him: strength and beauty are in his sanctuary” (Psalm 96:6)
summary: David’s song in 1 Chronicles 16 and Psalm 96 share this verse. 1 Chronicles 16:27 has glory and honour, and then strength and gladness in his place; Psalm 96:6 has honour and majesty, and then strength and beauty in his sanctuary.
text: KJV 1 Chronicles 16:27: “Glory and honour are in his presence; strength and gladness are in his place.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 16:27: הֹ֤וד וְהָדָר֙ לְפָנָ֔יו עֹ֥ז וְחֶדְוָ֖ה בִּמְקֹמֹֽו׃. KJV Psalm 96:6: “Honour and majesty are before him: strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 96:6: הֹוד־וְהָדָ֥ר לְפָנָ֑יו עֹ֥ז וְ֝תִפְאֶ֗רֶת בְּמִקְדָּשֹֽׁו׃. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/1CH16.htm and https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/PSA096.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/16/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/96/.
reasoning: The two verses have the same shape and three of the same Hebrew words, but they name different things. The first pair is “glory and honour” (הוֹד וְהָדָר) in 1 Chronicles, and in Psalm 96 the Hebrew has the same two words and the KJV prints them “honour and majesty”. The second pair is “strength and gladness” (עֹז וְחֶדְוָה) in 1 Chronicles and “strength and beauty” (עֹז וְתִפְאֶרֶת) in Psalm 96. The place is “his place” (בִּמְקוֹמוֹ) in one and “his sanctuary” (בְּמִקְדָּשׁוֹ) in the other. Gladness and beauty, and a place and a sanctuary, are different things.
scope: This sets the same verse in two books beside each other as the KJV gives them. It does not say either book is wrong, or which came first; the first pair of Hebrew words is the same and only the KJV’s English differs there, and that is not claimed as a difference of meaning. Psalm 96:5 has its own published record. Only the KJV and the Hebrew wording of the verses were compared. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.
